questions.question: What are the four pillars of OOP and how does Java implement each?
questions.title: Four Pillars of OOP in Java
questions.direct_answer: The four commonly taught OOP pillars are encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction. Java supports them with access control and class APIs, `extends`, overriding and interfaces, and contracts that hide implementation details. These ideas often work together, but one line of code does not have to demonstrate all four.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can explain each OOP idea with a correct Java mechanism and a concrete example.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reciting slogans such as 'interface is 100% abstraction' or claiming one statement automatically uses all four pillars.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the boundary of each idea and show `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>()` as abstraction and subtype polymorphism without overclaiming.

sections.title: Four OOP Ideas and Their Java Mechanisms
sections.content:
The four commonly taught ideas are **encapsulation**, **inheritance**, **polymorphism**, and **abstraction**. They describe different design concerns rather than four features that every class must use.

- **Encapsulation** keeps an object's representation behind a controlled API. A `BankAccount` can keep `balance` private and allow changes only through `deposit` and `withdraw`.
- **Inheritance** lets a class extend one superclass and reuse or specialize accessible behavior. It models a genuine subtype relationship, not merely a shortcut for copying code.
- **Polymorphism** lets code use a common type while overridden instance methods run according to the actual object. Java also uses the term compile-time polymorphism for overloading, although overloading is method selection by the compiler.
- **Abstraction** presents the operations callers need while hiding changeable details. Interfaces, abstract classes, ordinary classes, and composition can all create useful abstractions.

For example, `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();` clearly demonstrates abstraction and subtype polymorphism: the caller programs to `List`, while the object is an `ArrayList`. It does not by itself prove that inheritance or encapsulation is used well inside the implementation.

sections.title: Four Pillars — Java Mechanism Under Each
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    OOP["Four OOP design ideas"]
    OOP --> E["Encapsulation"]
    OOP --> I["Inheritance"]
    OOP --> P["Polymorphism"]
    OOP --> A["Abstraction"]
    E --> E1["Private representation plus controlled operations"]
    I --> I1["extends for a genuine subtype"]
    P --> P1["Override selected from the actual object"]
    A --> A1["Caller sees a useful contract"]
```

Interfaces may contain abstract, default, static, and private methods. Abstraction is therefore about the API boundary, not a percentage of methods without bodies.

sections.title: All Four Pillars in One Example
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating each pillar as one keyword:** a useful abstraction or encapsulated design comes from the API boundary, not merely writing `interface` or `private`.
- **Calling every interface '100% abstract':** interfaces may contain default, static, and private methods.
- **Confusing overloading and overriding:** overload selection is compile-time; overridden instance methods use runtime dispatch.
- **Claiming one declaration proves all four:** `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>()` directly shows abstraction and subtype polymorphism, not every design property.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Encapsulation:** protect representation behind a focused API.
- **Inheritance:** extend one superclass for a real subtype relationship.
- **Polymorphism:** the same common type can represent objects with different overridden behavior.
- **Abstraction:** expose useful operations and hide changeable details.
- **Use them deliberately:** not every class or statement needs all four.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The four commonly taught OOP pillars are encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction. Encapsulation means an object controls access to its representation—for example, a bank account keeps its balance private and validates changes through methods. Inheritance lets a class extend one superclass when it truly is a subtype. Polymorphism lets a caller use a parent type or interface while an overridden instance method runs for the actual object. Abstraction gives callers a useful contract without requiring them to know the implementation.

For example, `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();` shows abstraction and runtime substitutability: my code depends on the `List` operations, and I can choose an `ArrayList` implementation. I would not claim that this single line proves all four pillars. In real code the ideas are tools: I use inheritance only for a stable subtype relationship, keep state behind clear operations, and depend on the smallest useful abstraction.

questions.question: What is the difference between composition and inheritance in Java?
questions.title: Composition vs Inheritance in Java
questions.direct_answer: Inheritance creates a subtype relationship: `Dog extends Animal`. Composition builds a class from collaborators: `Car` holds an `Engine`. Composition often reduces dependence on a base class and allows collaborators to be replaced, but it is not automatically loose coupling—the field type and exposed behavior still decide the coupling.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the IS-A vs HAS-A test and why composition is usually the safer default.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reaching for inheritance just to reuse code, creating fragile deep hierarchies and breaking the IS-A test.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the fragile base class problem and that composition lets you swap behaviour at runtime (strategy pattern).

sections.title: Two Ways to Reuse Code — and Why One Is Usually Safer
sections.content:
**Inheritance** says one class is a subtype of another. A `Dog` can extend `Animal` when every `Dog` can be used wherever an `Animal` is expected. The subclass receives accessible behavior and can override permitted instance methods. This also ties it to the superclass contract and to protected implementation decisions.

**Composition** says an object works with another object. A `Car` can hold an `Engine` and delegate `start()` to it. If the field is typed as a small `Engine` interface and supplied through the constructor, the car can work with different implementations. If it is typed directly as one large concrete class, composition can still be tightly coupled.

'Favor composition over inheritance' is a design guideline, not a ban on inheritance. Prefer composition for optional or replaceable behavior and inheritance for a stable, documented subtype relationship. Judge both by the public contract and how likely the dependency is to change.

sections.title: IS-A (extends) vs HAS-A (field reference)
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Inheritance ["IS-A — Inheritance (extends)"] direction TB Animal["Animal
+ name: String
+ sound(): String"] Dog["Dog
extends Animal
+ sound(): String"] Animal -->|"extends"| Dog end subgraph Composition ["HAS-A — Composition (field)"] direction TB Car["Car
- engine: Engine
+ start()"] Engine["Engine
+ ignite()"] Car -->|"has a (field)"| Engine end ``` Inheritance: the arrow goes up (parent → child). Composition: the arrow goes sideways (owner → part). The direction tells you the coupling direction — inheritance locks the child to the parent's internals; composition keeps the owner in control.

sections.title: Composition vs Inheritance — When to Use Each
sections.content:
| Aspect | Inheritance | Composition |
|---|---|---|
| **Relationship** | IS-A (`extends`) | HAS-A (field reference) |
| **Coupling** | Tight — child depends on parent internals | Loose — owner controls what it exposes |
| **Flexibility** | Fixed at compile time | Swappable at runtime |
| **Reuse via** | Automatic via `extends` | Explicit delegation |
| **Parent limit** | One parent class only | Compose as many objects as needed |
| **API exposure** | Child inherits parent's full public API | Only delegated methods are visible |
| **Risk** | Fragile base class — parent change breaks children | A bit more boilerplate |
| **Use when** | Genuine IS-A, subclasses are substitutable | Reusing code without IS-A, or need runtime swap |

sections.title: Queue — Inheritance Misused, then Fixed with Composition
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reaching for `extends` purely to reuse code** — inheritance without a genuine IS-A relationship couples you to the parent's internals and leaks its entire public API to your callers.
- **Skipping the IS-A test** — `class Queue extends Stack` looks convenient, but a queue is not a stack; callers can call inherited `pop()` or insert in the middle and break the queue's contract.
- **Ignoring Java's single-parent limit** — once you `extends` one class for reuse, a second shared behavior forces an awkward rewrite, whereas composition lets you hold as many fields as you need.
- **Assuming a base-class change is safe** — editing a parent method can silently break every subclass that relied on its internals; this is the fragile base class problem that composition sidesteps.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Inheritance:** `extends`; use for a genuine subtype relationship.
- **Composition:** hold and delegate to a collaborator.
- **Coupling depends on the contract:** composition is not automatically loose.
- **Flexibility:** constructor-injected interface collaborators can be replaced without changing the owner.
- **Guideline:** favor composition for reuse alone; keep inheritance for stable subtyping.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Inheritance models an is-a relationship. If `Dog extends Animal`, code that accepts an `Animal` should be able to use a `Dog` without special cases. Composition models collaboration: a `Car` has an `Engine` field and delegates engine work to it.

I usually choose composition when behavior should be optional, replaceable, or combined from several collaborators. For example, a `CheckoutService` that receives a `PaymentGateway` interface can use a test gateway or a production gateway without subclassing the service. That is loose coupling because of the small interface and injection—not merely because a field exists. I choose inheritance when the parent defines a stable subtype contract and subclassing is intentionally supported. The guideline is to avoid extending a class only to borrow code, because superclass changes can affect subclasses in ways composition can contain.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Queue / Stack misuse, then a Car / Engine composition in Java
speakable_v2.hook: Reaching for `extends` just to grab a few methods? That's how a Queue quietly turns into a Stack.

groups.heading: Inheritance (IS-A)
groups.text: A child `extends` a parent and grabs its members. Tight coupling, fixed early. It models is-a.

groups.heading: Composition (HAS-A)
groups.text: An owner holds another object as a field and delegates. Loose coupling. The split's really has-a versus is-a.

beats.text: Run the IS-A test before you write `extends`. Ask if 'X is a Y' truly holds everywhere. If it doesn't, compose instead. Keep inheritance for when the subclass really substitutes for its parent.

Classic gotcha: `class Queue extends Stack`. A queue isn't a stack. Extending leaks the whole Stack API, so callers can call `pop`. The fix? Hold a private `Deque` and expose only enqueue and dequeue.

speakable_v2.cap: So favour composition over inheritance. Reach for `extends` only when IS-A truly holds and the subclass really fits its parent.
